INTRODUCTION
 I. I MEET SIR HENRY CURTIS
 II. THE LEGEND OF SOLOMON’S MINES
 III. UMBOPA ENTERS OUR SERVICE
 IV. AN ELEPHANT HUNT
 V. OUR MARCH INTO THE DESERT
 VI. WATER! WATER!
 VII. SOLOMON’S ROAD
 VIII. WE ENTER KUKUANALAND
 IX. TWALA THE KING
 X. THE WITCH-HUNT
 XI. WE GIVE A SIGN
 XII. BEFORE THE BATTLE
 XIII. THE ATTACK
 XIV. THE LAST STAND OF THE GREYS
 XV. GOOD FALLS SICK
 XVI. THE PLACE OF DEATH
 XVII. SOLOMON’S TREASURE CHAMBER
 XVIII. WE ABANDON HOPE
 XIX. IGNOSI’S FAREWELL
 XX. FOUND


PREPARER’S NOTE

This was typed from a 1907 edition published by Cassell and Company,
Limited.




DEDICATION

This faithful but unpretending record
of a remarkable adventure
is hereby respectfully dedicated
by the narrator,

ALLAN QUATERMAIN,

to all the big and little boys
who read it.




AUTHOR’S NOTE


The author ventures to take this opportunity to thank his readers for
the kind reception they have accorded to the successive editions of
this tale during the last twelve years. He hopes that in its present
form it will fall into the hands of an even wider public, and that in
years to come it may continue to afford amusement to those who are
still young enough at heart to love a story of treasure, war, and wild
adventure.

Ditchingham,
11 March, 1898.




POST SCRIPTUM


Now, in 1907, on the occasion of the issue of this edition, I can only
add how glad I am that my romance should continue to please so many
readers. Imagination has been verified by fact; the King Solomon’s
Mines I dreamed of have been discovered, and are putting out their gold
once more, and, according to the latest reports, their diamonds also;
the Kukuanas or, rather, the Matabele, have been tamed by the white
man’s bullets, but still there seem to be many who find pleasure in
these simple pages. That they may continue so to do, even to the third
and fourth generation, or perhaps longer still, would, I am sure, be
the hope of our old and departed friend, Allan Quatermain.

H. Rider Haggard.
Ditchingham, 1907.

This unvarnished, no-frills record of the most harrowing trek I ever survived in decades roaming the South African bush unfolds beat for beat as it happened, no embellishments added, no dangers softened:
1.  My first fateful meeting with Sir Henry Curtis, the wealthy English gentleman who would risk everything to track down his lost missing brother
2.  The ancient, half-forgotten legend of King Solomon’s fabled diamond mines — sealed away for centuries beyond uncrossable deserts and the borders of a kingdom no white man had ever set foot in
3.  The tall, quiet stranger named Umbopa who walked out of the savanna to ask for work, carrying a secret far larger than any of us guessed at the time
4.  The high-stakes elephant hunt that spiraled out of control, leaving one of our party grievously wounded before we even reached the edge of the desert
5.  The brutal, sun-scorched march across miles of unbroken red sand, where every step felt like it could be our last
6.  The mad, desperate scramble for water when our canteens ran dry and we were hours away from dying of heatstroke
7.  The half-ruined, ancient stone road no outsider had trod in a thousand years: Solomon’s own highway, leading straight to his hidden realm
8.  The moment we crossed the snow-capped mountain pass and stepped into Kukuanaland, a kingdom the outside world had no idea existed
9.  Twala, the brutal one-eyed king who ruled Kukuanaland with iron fists and the cruel magic of his witch advisors
10. The horrific kingdom-wide witch-hunt that nearly got all three of us executed as evil interlopers
11. The impossible feat we pulled off to prove we were not sorcerers, and turn thousands of Twala’s own warriors to our side
12. The tense days of waiting for battle, knowing an army of spear-wielding fighters a hundred times our size was marching to kill us
13. The first clash of armies, where a tiny band of rebels held their ground against overwhelming royal forces
14. The last, blood-soaked stand of the Greys, the king’s legendary elite regiment, that left the battlefields soaked in iron-red blood
15. The vicious fever that seized our party’s Captain Good, nearly taking his life right when we stood on the cusp of finding the mines
16. The Place of Death: the hidden valley of weathered bones that marked the entrance to Solomon’s long-lost treasure vaults
17. The moment we stepped inside the fabled treasure chamber, and saw more gold and uncut diamonds than any of us had ever dared to dream existed
18. The hours we spent trapped behind a sealed stone door, certain we would die in total darkness, our names and our discovery never known to the outside world
19. The bittersweet goodbye we shared with Umbopa, who revealed himself as Kukuanaland’s rightful heir and took his place as the new king
20. The final, improbable twist that saw us stumble back to civilization alive, with sacks of diamonds heavy enough to make every one of us rich for life.

---
This edition is typed faithfully from the 1907 original printing released by Cassell and Company, Limited.

This plain, unpolished record of a one-of-a-kind African adventure is respectfully dedicated by its narrator, Allan Quatermain, to every boy big and small who loves stories of wild untamed places, high stakes, and buried treasure.

Twelve years have passed since this tale first reached print, and I owe all my readers a deep debt of gratitude for the warm welcome they have given every successive new edition. I hope this new form will find its way to an even wider public, and that for decades to come, it will continue to bring joy to everyone young enough at heart to love a story of treasure, war, and wild unscripted adventure.
H. Rider Haggard
Ditchingham, 11 March 1898

Now, on the release of this new 1907 edition, I can only add how overjoyed I am that this old romance still pleases so many readers. Imagination has been verified by fact: the King Solomon’s Mines I dreamed of all those years ago have been discovered, spilling out their gold once more, and per the latest reports, vast stores of diamonds too. The Kukuanas, or their kin the Matabele, have been tamed by the white man’s rifles, but still, countless readers keep returning to these simple pages. That they may continue to delight people even to the third and fourth generation, and longer still, is a hope I know our old, departed friend Allan Quatermain shared wholeheartedly.
H. Rider Haggard
Ditchingham, 1907
